t: Users With Two Purchases Within Seven Days — Self Join vs Window Function
o: We need every user who has some pair of purchases dated at most 7 days apart; same-day purchases qualify since 0 <= 7. In the sample, user 2 qualifies through 2022-03-13 and 2022-03-20 (exactly 7 days apart), user 7 qualifies through two purchases on 2022-06-19, and user 5's single purchase never forms a pair. The comparison must happen between rows of the same user, which suggests either joining the table to itself on user_id or walking each user's dates in order with LAG. Because one user can produce many qualifying pairs, duplicates must be collapsed before returning user_id, and the output is ordered by user_id.
k: Only intra-user date pairs matter, so join or partition by user_id before comparing dates.
DATEDIFF(b.purchase_date, a.purchase_date) BETWEEN 0 AND 7 counts each pair once (later minus earlier) and naturally includes same-day pairs.
If any pair is within 7 days, then some adjacent pair in each user's sorted dates is too, so checking consecutive LAG gaps suffices.
A qualifying user usually appears multiple times, hence DISTINCT (or grouping the window subquery) is mandatory.

a.i: Join Purchases to itself on user_id with the condition that the second row's date is 0 to 7 days after the first's. Any qualifying pair survives the join, so the set of surviving user_ids is exactly the answer; DISTINCT removes the repetition caused by users with several close purchases. This is the most direct relational formulation of 'some two purchases at most 7 days apart'.
s: Alias the table twice (a for the earlier purchase, b for the later one).
Join ON a.user_id = b.user_id AND DATEDIFF(b.purchase_date, a.purchase_date) BETWEEN 0 AND 7.
Select DISTINCT a.user_id to deduplicate repeated qualifying pairs.

c.python:
# LeetCode 2228 is a SQL problem; the accepted solution is the MySQL query below.
MYSQL_SOLUTION = """
SELECT DISTINCT a.user_id
FROM Purchases a
JOIN Purchases b
  ON a.user_id = b.user_id
 AND DATEDIFF(b.purchase_date, a.purchase_date) BETWEEN 0 AND 7
ORDER BY user_id;
"""

a.t: O(P^2) worst case per user group — the self join compares all row pairs sharing a user_id (P = number of purchases).
a.sp: O(P) — intermediate join result bounded by pair counts.

a.n: Approach 2: LAG Window Function Over Sorted Dates
a.i: Sort each user's purchase dates chronologically and compute the gap to the previous purchase with LAG. If any pair lies within 7 days, adjacent dates between them accumulate gaps summing to at most 7, so at least one consecutive gap is <= 7 — scanning only adjacent gaps is sufficient. Filtering the computed gaps keeps one row per qualifying purchase, and DISTINCT flattens to unique users. This reads each row once and lets the engine avoid quadratic pairing.
s: In a subquery, partition by user_id ordered by purchase_date.
Keep rows where diff <= 7 (the first purchase's NULL gap fails this automatically).
Select DISTINCT user_id from the filtered rows and order by user_id.

c.python:
# LeetCode 2228 is a SQL problem; the accepted solution is the MySQL query below.
MYSQL_SOLUTION = """
SELECT DISTINCT user_id
FROM (
    SELECT user_id,
           DATEDIFF(purchase_date,
                    LAG(purchase_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY purchase_date)) AS diff
    FROM Purchases
) t
WHERE diff <= 7
ORDER BY user_id;
"""

a.t: O(P log P) — sorting/partitioning purchases by user and date dominates.

w: Offer the LAG solution as primary (linear-ish, idiomatic modern SQL) with the self join as the classic fallback that works even on very old engines lacking window functions. Pitfalls: using ABS(datediff) in the join doubles every pair and still needs DISTINCT; forgetting DATEDIFF argument order flips signs so nothing passes diff <= 7; NULL from LAG on a user's first purchase silently drops out under <= comparisons, which is desired here. Edge cases: same-day duplicate purchases (gap 0 qualifies) and exactly-7-day gaps (inclusive). Follow-ups: report the minimum gap per user with MIN(diff), or restrict to purchases within a rolling window.
